- Basal Body Temperature is the lowest body temperature attained during rest (usually during sleep)
- It is measured using a special thermometer available at the chemist
- For better accuracy, it has to be recorded at the same time every day. Preferably, right after you wake up, even before you step out of bed
- There will be a slight rise in temperature around the fertile days, which indicates ovulation. To understand this pattern, it is advisable to chart your temperature for at least three cycles

Maya says: Be thorough in recording all data. Make sure you record both start and end dates of your period. You can log a range of notes, including symptoms and moods in the notes section. Jot down any notes you think might be useful in the future.

Maya says: If the arrival of your periods are highly unpredictable, it might be advisable to consult a physician. Before you dash to the doctor, apply the three-cycle rule. Get a check-up if changes last for three cycles in a row or if your period is delayed by more than 10 days.
Maya says: Restoring emotional and physical balance in your life can help. Many women miss their periods occasionally. Unless you are pregnant, chances are your cycle will return to normal soon.

Maya says: Your doctor can properly diagnose the reason for your late or missed period. Keep a record of all cycle related information in Maya. Make it a habit to log notes everyday. Presenting this data to doctors will help them make an accurate diagnosis.
Maya says: If your cycle is delayed for more than 10 days, consult a doctor. On start of a new cycle, enter the date into Maya so that predictions will resume.

Maya says: If you have a mild case of the blues, chase it away with a comedy or funny book. Laughter is not just the best medicine, it’s the easiest and simplest form of exercise and has the health benefits of a mild workout. A few minutes of laughter will relieve tension and leave your muscles relaxed for almost 45 minutes.

Maya says: Unless you’re trying for a baby, be extra careful as you’re highly susceptible to pregnancy. In fact, you’re most fertile one to two days before ovulation, so be sure you have everything covered.

Maya says: You’ll probably notice your temperature spiking on other days, but unless it stays that way for at least three days in a row you’re probably not ovulating. Remember that if you are ill, or forget to take your temperature immediately on waking, any pattern you find may be inaccurate.

Maya says: Worry not, as the percentage of men who can actually decipher this is very small! Clear your calendar of big social events and make a date with yourself. A hot Epsom salt bath soak is a great place to start, as it can have amazing health benefits like improved circulation and stress relief.

Maya says: As a girl gets older and her periods settle down - or she gets used to her own unique cycle - she will probably find that she can predict when her period will come. In the meantime, it’s a good idea to keep track of your menstrual cycle with the calendar in Maya.
Maya says: Place a hot water bottle or heating pads on your lower belly and lower back. You could also soak in a warm bath to alleviate the discomfort.

Maya says: Kick back with a cup of chamomile or jasmine tea. An amino acid in chamomile helps reduce muscle contractions in the uterus, lessen bloating and fight insomnia. Jasmine flowers are famous for their soothing and relaxing effect on the stomach and the mind.
Maya says: Change sanitary pads or tampons regularly, at least every four hours. And remember to record the date when your period stops on Maya. This will make predictions more accurate.

Maya says: Get moving. The more physically active you are, the less likely you are to suffer from chronic aches and pains, including menstrual cramps. Cardio is good for increasing blood flow throughout your body and this in turn reduces discomfort or pain.

Maya says: During your period, washing more than once a day may be helpful. Keeping the whole genital region clean is essential to keep infections away. Wash the area at least once a day during your normal bathing routines.
Maya says: Fiber can keep gastric problems under control. Aim for 30 grams a day from cereal, fruit and vegetables. Remember to hydrate yourself with plenty of water.
Maya says: Indulge yourself with a massage, meditate, or learn a new hobby. Strenuous exercise will feel increasingly good during this time, so get out and enjoy physical activities that you love.

Maya says: Talk with your doctor if you suspect menorrhagia. Since flow volumes vary for each individual, it is difficult to self diagnose. Log notes related to flow to provide your doctor with accurate inputs.

Maya says: Talk to a friend about the issue, and take them along to the doctor’s. The solution might be a simple one, but it can stop the situation from developing into a serious underlying health issue.

Maya says: Keeping a daily record is incredibly beneficial. You will see that Maya learns about your monthly cycle over time and predicts dates more accurately. Soon you’ll have all the information you or your doctor need at your fingertips.
Maya says: Crash diets are a no-no. Good nutrition means eating a wide variety of foods in moderation every day, to get all the nutrients your body needs.
Maya says: Create a playlist with your favorite music, and go for a run in the park. It will leave you feeling high and frisky. Log personal notes about your body and mind on Maya.

Maya says: Get your iron from red meat, chicken, fish, fortified cereals, legumes and nuts and green leafy vegetables. Absorption can be impaired by very high-fibre diets, alcohol, the tannic acid in tea and concentrated courses of calcium (like calcium supplements).

First-trimester prenatal tests

Many prenatal tests are for screening rather than diagnostic purposes. Screening tests give you a sense of your risk for certain conditions. But only a diagnostic test can tell you for sure whether your baby has a problem. Here are some of the options during the first trimester:

"First-trimester screening: First-trimester screening includes a blood test that measures the levels of two proteins in your blood and a special ultrasound scan. The scan is performed between 11 weeks of pregnancy through the end of 13 weeks, and the blood test may be done at the same time or a few weeks earlier. This gives you information about your baby's odds of having Down syndrome and a few other conditions. This screening is not diagnostic, is risk-free and may help you decide whether you want invasive diagnostic testing such as CVS, which carry a slight risk of miscarriage."

Noninvasive Prenatal Testing: Another alternative is a blood test that can detect Down syndrome and a few other chromosomal conditions at 10 weeks of pregnancy or later. NIPT is available to all women but is usually tested on women at high risk of having a baby with a chromosomal condition. NIPT is a screening test, which means that if the results indicate a problem, you will need a CVS diagnosis.

CVS: This diagnostic test involves collecting cells from the placenta, which are then sent to a lab for genetic analysis. CVS can identify whether your baby has any of hundreds of chromosomal abnormalities and other genetic disorders. It is done in the first trimester, usually between 10 and 12 weeks.
